newsitem.title: SPAIN: SOCCER SHOWCASE-FOREIGN 'KEEPERS DEFY CRITICS AND WIN OVER FANS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-FOREIGN 'KEEPERS DEFY CRITICS AND WIN OVER FANS.

text.p: The arrival of Barcelona 'keeper Vitor Baia and Real Madrid counterpart Bodo Illgner raised more than a few eyebrows in Spain over the summer.
But it is a sign of the quality of both men that the initial fuss has died down, and they are being cast as key figures ahead of Saturday's big Real-Barcelona clash.
That is no mean achievement in a country that prides itself on the quality of its own goalkeepers.
Several critics had hit out at the signings, saying Spanish 'keepers were just as good as their rivals and foreigners were being bought for the sake of it.

But Baia and Illgner -- who lead a group of six foreigners who have taken up residence between the posts at Spanish first division sides -- have silenced the hawks who were ready to pounce on their slightest mistakes.
Baia's perfomances, in particular, have been spectacular.

Most commentators had concluded Barcelona needed a new keeper after a season in which the handball-style goalkeeping of Carlos Busquets, who relied heavily on making saves with his legs, had cost the side more than a few moments of panic.
But few people believed Baia could justify the 800 million peseta ($6.1 million) fee. For many, the signing was simply a whim of new coach Bobby Robson, Baia's former manager at Porto.

But the elegant Baia, who already speaks excellent Spanish, has impressed fans on and off the pitch. And he has solved a goalkeeping problem at Nou Camp that dates back to 1994 when Spanish international Andoni Zubizarreta left for Valencia.
Illgner's linguistic progress has been less impressive than Baia's but his work between the posts has been just as effective.

The former international, who resigned his place in the German side after the 1994 World Cup, has had the unenviable task of displacing two 'keepers who would find a place in practically any club side and many national teams.
At 38, Paco Buyo was continuing to defy not only age and gravity, but also the aspirations of Santiago Canizares, the 'dauphin' to Zubizarreta in the Spanish national team.
Canizares had shot to prominence by saving Spain in a vital World Cup game in 1993 after coming on as substitute, but had been relegated to the bench after moving to Madrid from Celta Vigo.
So when Capello announced this summer he needed a taller keeper, Canizares, Buyo and Real fans everywhere were stunned.
But Illgner has quietly got on with his work and gradually won over even the most sceptical of the Santiago Bernabeu faithful.
Even so, both Illgner and Baia know the importance of Real-Barcelona games means a mistake on Saturday would undo a lot of their good work.
